Blog Post 1


Simpson’s Paradox: When Every Group Tells One Story and the Total Tells Another


An admissions example reveals how unequal group sizes reverse a comparison—and how to interpret the result responsibly.





Sep 14, 2026





No matching items

title: Blog Post 1
text:
Imagine a university with two departments: one less selective and one more selective. Applicants belong to Group A or Group B. A headline reports that 36% of Group A applicants were admitted, compared with 74% of Group B. That looks like a major advantage for B.
But inside each department, A has the higher admission rate. How can A do better everywhere and still do worse overall?
This is Simpson’s paradox: an association can reverse when we combine groups. It challenges our instinct that a consistent pattern in every part must survive in the whole. The problem is not faulty arithmetic; it is a change in who receives the most weight.

title: Blog Post 1
section: Build the puzzle from four rows
text:
Build the puzzle from four rows
All counts below are invented for this explanation, not real university records. There are 100 applicants in each group. The labels describe only department selectivity; we have no information about applicants’ qualifications.


Show reproducible R code
# All data are defined here; no downloads or random simulation are needed.
admissions <- data.frame(
  group = c("A", "B", "A", "B"),
  department = c("Less selective", "Less selective",
                 "More selective", "More selective"),
  applicants = c(10, 90, 90, 10),
  admitted = c(9, 72, 27, 2)
)
admissions$rate <- admissions$admitted / admissions$applicants

within_table <- data.frame(
  Department = admissions$department,
  Group = admissions$group,
  Applicants = admissions$applicants,
  Admitted = admissions$admitted,
  `Admission rate` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * admissions$rate),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(within_table,
             caption = "Synthetic admissions counts and within-department rates.")

totals <- aggregate(cbind(applicants, admitted) ~ group,

In the less selective department, A leads 90% to 80%. In the more selective department, A leads 30% to 20%. Both differences are ten percentage points. Yet overall, A admits 36 of 100 applicants and B admits 74 of 100. B’s aggregate advantage is 38 percentage points.


Show reproducible R code
rates <- rbind(
  A = c(admissions$rate[1], admissions$rate[3], totals$rate[totals$group == "A"]),
  B = c(admissions$rate[2], admissions$rate[4], totals$rate[totals$group == "B"])
)
colnames(rates) <- c("Less selective", "More selective", "Overall")
local({
  previous <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  on.exit(par(previous))
  positions <- barplot(100 * rates, beside = TRUE,
    col = c("#246B8E", "#D07629"), border = NA, ylim = c(0, 112),
    ylab = "Admission rate (%)", las = 1)
  text(positions, 100 * rates + 4,
       labels = paste0(round(100 * rates), "%"), cex = 0.9)
  legend("topright", legend = c("Group A", "Group B"),
         fill = c("#246B8E", "#D07629"), bty = "n", horiz = TRUE)
})








Figure 1: A leads within both departments, but B leads overall. All panels use the same percentage scale; the overall bars pool counts rather than averaging departmental rates equally.

title: Blog Post 1
text:
The hidden ingredient: different weights
Most A applicants choose the harder department, whereas most B applicants choose the easier one. Each overall rate is a weighted average: a department’s weight is its share of that group’s applicants.

\begin{aligned}
R_A &= 0.10(0.90) + 0.90(0.30) = 0.36,\\
R_B &= 0.90(0.80) + 0.10(0.20) = 0.74.
\end{aligned}

Picture two baskets of exam scores. One basket contains mostly difficult exams; the other contains mostly easy exams. Comparing basket averages mixes performance with exam difficulty. Admissions rates work the same way: the overall comparison mixes within-department outcomes with application patterns.
This explains the surprise. We mentally compare A and B using the same departmental mix, but the aggregate calculation uses different mixes. Having the same total number of applicants does not solve this problem. Their distribution across departments matters.

title: Blog Post 1
section: Compare the groups using a common mix
text:
Compare the groups using a common mix
We can separate the composition effect by giving both groups the same weights. Across all applicants, half apply to each department, so a 50–50 reference mix is natural here.


Show reproducible R code
# Common weights come from the pooled applicant distribution.
reference <- aggregate(applicants ~ department, admissions, sum)
reference$weight <- reference$applicants / sum(reference$applicants)
weighted_data <- merge(admissions, reference[c("department", "weight")],
                       by = "department")
weighted_data$contribution <- weighted_data$rate * weighted_data$weight
adjusted <- aggregate(contribution ~ group, weighted_data, sum)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Group = adjusted$group,
  `Rate with a common departmental mix` =
    sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * adjusted$contribution),
  check.names = FALSE
), caption = "Standardized rates answer a different question from observed overall rates.")



Standardized rates answer a different question from observed overall rates.


Group
Rate with a common departmental mix

Show reproducible R code
# Verify the numerical claims and the reversal.
stopifnot(all(admissions$admitted <= admissions$applicants),
          isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(totals$rate), c(0.36, 0.74))),
          all(rates[1, 1:2] > rates[2, 1:2]),
          isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(adjusted$contribution), c(0.60, 0.50))))


Now A’s standardized rate is 60% and B’s is 50%. These are hypothetical rates calculated by retaining each group’s departmental rates while imposing a common application mix. They are not additional observed admissions or predictions about what would happen if applicants changed departments.

title: Blog Post 1
section: Which comparison answers the right question?
text:
Which comparison answers the right question?
For “What fraction of each group’s actual applicants was admitted?”, the overall rates are correct. For “How do their rates compare within departments?”, use the departmental rates. For “How do they compare under a common departmental mix?”, standardized rates are useful. No arithmetic result contradicts another; each answers a different question.
None proves discrimination, fairness, or a causal effect of group membership. Qualifications and other selection processes remain unobserved. Department choice could itself reflect unequal access, so adjusting for it might conceal part of the mechanism we care about. Choosing what to condition on requires understanding the process, not automatically splitting every dataset into smaller groups.

title: Blog Post 1
text:
A lesson beyond this example
Simpson’s 1951 paper examined relationships in contingency tables. Admissions also became a famous application in Bickel, Hammel, and O’Connell’s Berkeley study. Our deliberately simplified numbers are not taken from either paper. They demonstrate an exact arithmetic reversal, not a statistical estimate; there are no confidence intervals or claims about a real population.






NoteTakeaway



Before trusting an overall comparison, inspect subgroup rates and their denominators. Ask whether different group compositions drive the result, then choose the comparison that fits your question. A convincing explanation needs the rates, the weights, and the context.

title: Blog Post 2
text:
America’s most famous national parks can also be its busiest. A traveler who values open space might ask: Which established parks in the contiguous United States combine substantial visitation with relatively low visitor pressure? Rather than naming my favorite park, I will build a transparent shortlist from two measurable quantities: annual recreation visits and park area.
My metric is annual visits per 1,000 acres. A smaller number means more park acreage relative to recorded visits. It is a screening tool—not a literal count of people someone will meet. Visitors cluster at popular trails, arrive in different seasons, and may enter the same park more than once.

title: Blog Post 2
text:
One respectful request
I scraped the Wikipedia list of U.S. national parks on September 20, 2026. Its table reports 2023 acreage and 2025 recreation visits, citing National Park Service sources. Wikipedia text is available under CC BY-SA 4.0, and this post attributes and links the source rather than copying its prose or images. I also checked Wikipedia’s robots.txt: this ordinary article path is not disallowed. The analysis sends one request, accesses no login or restricted page, and does not crawl individual park pages.
As a provenance check, I compared the scraped leaders with the official NPS Annual Visitation by Park report. The 2025 totals match exactly: Death Valley 1,320,134, Everglades 778,198, and Big Bend 568,104. These are recreation visits, not unique people. The NPS portal remains the appropriate place to verify later revisions before booking.


Show reproducible R code
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_parks_of_the_United_States"

# One HTTP request; select the first table by its semantic CSS class.
page <- read_html(url)
raw <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table(fill = TRUE)

# Footnote numbers in column names can change, so locate columns by prefix.
area_col <- names(raw)[str_detect(names(raw), "^Area")][1]
visit_col <- names(raw)[str_detect(names(raw), "^Recreation visitors")][1]
stopifnot(!is.na(area_col), !is.na(visit_col))

parks <- raw |>
  transmute(
    park = Name |>
      str_remove_all("[†‡*]") |>
      str_squish(),
    location = Location |>
      str_remove("\\s*\\.mw-parser.*$") |>
      str_remove("\\s+\\d.*$") |>
      str_squish(),
    area_acres = parse_number(.data[[area_col]]),
    visits_2025 = parse_number(.data[[visit_col]])
  ) |>
  mutate(visits_per_1000_acres = visits_2025 / (area_acres / 1000))

# Fail loudly if the page structure or numeric parsing has broken.
stopifnot(nrow(parks) >= 60,
          all(!is.na(parks$area_acres)),
          all(!is.na(parks$visits_2025)),
          all(parks$area_acres > 0),
          all(parks$visits_2025 > 0))

# Archive the snapshot this post was built from, so the numbers reported here
# stay reproducible even after Wikipedia is edited.
write_csv(parks, "data/parks_clean.csv")


The scrape returns 63 parks. Separating extraction from cleaning makes the workflow auditable: html_table() collects text; parse_number() removes commas, units, and footnotes; and the checks stop the analysis instead of silently producing nonsense if the page changes.

title: Blog Post 2
text:
Define a useful comparison set
Huge, remote Alaskan parks naturally have very low density but may not suit an ordinary road trip. I therefore exclude Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories, then require at least 500,000 annual visits. The threshold is a simple proxy for an established destination, not a quality judgment. Changing it changes the choice set, so I report it explicitly.


Show reproducible R code
candidates <- parks |>
  filter(
    !str_detect(location, "Alaska|Hawaii|American Samoa|Virgin Islands"),
    visits_2025 >= 500000
  ) |>
  arrange(visits_per_1000_acres)

shortlist <- candidates |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  transmute(
    Park = park,
    Location = location,
    `2025 visits` = scales::comma(visits_2025),
    `Area (acres)` = scales::comma(round(area_acres)),
    `Visits per 1,000 acres` = scales::number(
      visits_per_1000_acres, accuracy = 1
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  shortlist,
  align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = "Lowest visitor pressure among established contiguous-U.S. candidates."
)

title: Blog Post 2
text:
What the comparison reveals


Show reproducible R code
top_eight <- candidates |> slice_head(n = 8)
reference_density <- median(candidates$visits_per_1000_acres)

ggplot(candidates, aes(area_acres, visits_2025)) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = reference_density / 1000,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed", color = "#8A8A8A"
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "#9CB9C8", size = 2.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = top_eight, color = "#C4512D", size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    data = top_eight,
    aes(label = park),
    nudge_y = 0.10,
    check_overlap = TRUE,
    size = 3.2,
    color = "#5B2B1E"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    x = "Park area (acres, log scale)",
    y = "2025 recreation visits (log scale)",
    title = "Large parks can absorb the same annual visitation differently",
    subtitle = "Candidates are contiguous-U.S. parks with at least 500,000 visits"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot")








Figure 1: Parks above the dashed line have more visits per 1,000 acres. Labels identify the eight lowest-pressure candidates; both axes are logarithmic so large and small parks remain visible.





Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend form the strongest initial shortlist. Death Valley has the lowest ratio in the filtered set: about 387 visits per 1,000 acres. By comparison, the candidate median is about 7,655. Everglades and Big Bend also combine more than half a million visits with large areas. For someone prioritizing space, I would investigate these three before defaulting to the most visited names.

title: Blog Post 2
text:
From ranking to action
The recommendation is to use this shortlist as stage one, then consult official park pages for road access, reservation rules, weather, closures, and seasonal visitation. For example, vast acreage can be wilderness, water, or otherwise inaccessible; annual totals cannot reveal congestion at one entrance at noon. The dataset counts visits rather than unique people and mixes two reference years (2023 area and 2025 visits). Wikipedia can also change after this post is rendered.
Those limitations do not make the analysis useless. They define what it can support: a low-cost way to narrow 63 possibilities, followed by local research. A stronger second stage would scrape or download monthly NPS visitation and compare the traveler’s intended month. That could distinguish a genuinely quieter trip window from a park that only looks spacious in an annual average.






ImportantActionable takeaway



For a crowd-averse contiguous-U.S. park trip, begin with Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, then verify season, access, and conditions with the NPS. The main analytical lesson is equally practical: rank options with a transparent denominator, state the filters, and never mistake acreage-adjusted annual visits for the experience at a particular trail or time.
